claim: Several hundred billion to trillion cells die in the human body every day.
source: Several hundred billion to trillion cells die in the human body every day (Fliedner et al., 2002; Sender and Milo, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Fliedner et al., 2002; Sender and Milo, 2021).

claim: Dying cells release chromosomal fragments in the form of cell-free chromatin particles (cfChPs).
source: Several hundred billion to trillion cells die in the human body every day (Fliedner et al., 2002; Sender and Milo, 2021) and release chromosomal fragments in the form of cell-free chromatin particles (cfChPs), which enter the extracellular compartments, including the circulation (Holdenrieder and Stieber, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Holdenrieder and Stieber, 2009).

claim: cfChPs circulating in the blood are readily internalised by living cells through horizontal transfer.
source: We previously reported that cfChPs circulating in the blood, and those that are released locally from dying cells, are readily internalised by living cells through horizontal transfer followed by their association with the host cell genome (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Internalised cfChPs associate with the host cell genome.
source: We previously reported that cfChPs circulating in the blood, and those that are released locally from dying cells, are readily internalised by living cells through horizontal transfer followed by their association with the host cell genome (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Association of cfChPs with the host cell genome was confirmed by whole-genome sequencing and fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) analysis.
source: The latter was confirmed by whole-genome sequencing and fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) analysis, as well as by the detection of multiple human Alu elements in the mouse recipient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to specific experimental methods used in previous work.

claim: Multiple human Alu elements were detected in mouse recipient cells after cfChPs treatment.
source: The latter was confirmed by whole-genome sequencing and fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) analysis, as well as by the detection of multiple human Alu elements in the mouse recipient cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to experimental findings from previous work.

claim: Cellular uptake of cfChPs induces DNA damage.
source: Cellular uptake of cfChPs has several biological ramifications such as induction of DNA damage and the activation of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Cellular uptake of cfChPs activates inflammatory pathways.
source: Cellular uptake of cfChPs has several biological ramifications such as induction of DNA damage and the activation of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Cellular uptake of cfChPs activates apoptotic pathways.
source: Cellular uptake of cfChPs has several biological ramifications such as induction of DNA damage and the activation of inflammatory and apoptotic pathways (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous publications (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: cfChPs isolated from cancer patients had significantly greater activity in terms of DNA damage than those isolated from healthy individuals.
source: We found that cfChPs isolated from cancer patients had significantly greater activity in terms of DNA damage and activation of apoptotic pathways than those isolated from healthy individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to findings from the authors' previous study (Mittra et al., 2015b).

claim: cfChPs isolated from cancer patients had significantly greater activity in terms of activation of apoptotic pathways than those isolated from healthy individuals.
source: We found that cfChPs isolated from cancer patients had significantly greater activity in terms of DNA damage and activation of apoptotic pathways than those isolated from healthy individuals.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to findings from the authors' previous study (Mittra et al., 2015b).

claim: cfChPs released locally from dying cells can horizontally transfer themselves into healthy bystander cells.
source: We have also reported that cfChPs released locally from dying cells can horizontally transfer themselves into healthy bystander cells, leading to DNA damage and inflammation (Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Horizontal transfer of cfChPs from dying cells to healthy bystander cells leads to DNA damage.
source: We have also reported that cfChPs released locally from dying cells can horizontally transfer themselves into healthy bystander cells, leading to DNA damage and inflammation (Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: Horizontal transfer of cfChPs from dying cells to healthy bystander cells leads to inflammation.
source: We have also reported that cfChPs released locally from dying cells can horizontally transfer themselves into healthy bystander cells, leading to DNA damage and inflammation (Mittra et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: cfChPs are rapidly and abundantly internalised by NIH3T3 mouse fibroblast cells.
source: Examination of NIH3T3 mouse fibroblasts treated with the dually fluorescently labelled cfChPs confirmed our earlier observation (Mittra et al., 2015b) that cfChPs can readily and rapidly horizontally transfer themselves to healthy cells via phagocytosis (Mittra et al., 2017) to accumulate in their cytoplasm and nuclei by 6 hr (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and citations to previous work (Mittra et al., 2015b; Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: cfChPs horizontally transfer themselves to healthy cells via phagocytosis.
source: Examination of NIH3T3 mouse fibroblasts treated with the dually fluorescently labelled cfChPs confirmed our earlier observation (Mittra et al., 2015b) that cfChPs can readily and rapidly horizontally transfer themselves to healthy cells via phagocytosis (Mittra et al., 2017) to accumulate in their cytoplasm and nuclei by 6 hr (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous publication (Mittra et al., 2017).

claim: cfChPs accumulate in the cytoplasm and nuclei of NIH3T3 cells by 6 hr after treatment.
source: Examination of NIH3T3 mouse fibroblasts treated with the dually fluorescently labelled cfChPs confirmed our earlier observation (Mittra et al., 2015b) that cfChPs can readily and rapidly horizontally transfer themselves to healthy cells via phagocytosis (Mittra et al., 2017) to accumulate in their cytoplasm and nuclei by 6 hr (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Multiple cfChPs amalgamate to form large concatemers following their cellular entry.
source: The fluorescent cfChPs appeared prominent, ostensibly owing to the amalgamation of multiple cfChPs to form large concatemers following their cellular entry (described in detail later).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed prominence of fluorescent signals and is described in detail later in the manuscript.

claim: Chromatin fibres prepared from cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed the presence of numerous dually labelled cfChPs of varying sizes.
source: Chromatin fibres prepared from similarly treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed the presence of numerous dually labelled cfChPs of varying sizes, which were present in both the cytoplasm and overlapping with mouse chromatin fibres (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Dually labelled cfChPs were present in both the cytoplasm and overlapping with mouse chromatin fibres.
source: Chromatin fibres prepared from similarly treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed the presence of numerous dually labelled cfChPs of varying sizes, which were present in both the cytoplasm and overlapping with mouse chromatin fibres (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Metaphase spreads prepared from cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed many dually labelled cfChPs.
source: Metaphase spreads prepared from cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed many dually labelled cfChPs, some of which were associated with the chromosomes while others were present in extrachromosomal spaces (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Some dually labelled cfChPs were associated with the chromosomes while others were present in extrachromosomal spaces.
source: Metaphase spreads prepared from cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells at 6 hr revealed many dually labelled cfChPs, some of which were associated with the chromosomes while others were present in extrachromosomal spaces (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: When cfChPs are horizontally transferred to another cell, the latter perceives the dsDNA breaks present in their two ends as damaged 'self' DNA.
source: We had earlier hypothesised that when the cfChPs are horizontally transferred to another cell, the latter perceives the dsDNA breaks present in their two ends as damaged 'self' DNA, and in an attempt to repair the 'perceived damage', activates proteins of the DDR pathway which links up multiple disparate cfChPs as a part of the repair process leading to the formation of concatemers of variable sizes (Mittra et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from the authors' previous work (Mittra et al., 2015b).

claim: In an attempt to repair the 'perceived damage', the host cell activates proteins of the DDR pathway which links up multiple disparate cfChPs leading to the formation of concatemers of variable sizes.
source: We had earlier hypothesised that when the cfChPs are horizontally transferred to another cell, the latter perceives the dsDNA breaks present in their two ends as damaged 'self' DNA, and in an attempt to repair the 'perceived damage', activates proteins of the DDR pathway which links up multiple disparate cfChPs as a part of the repair process leading to the formation of concatemers of variable sizes (Mittra et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from the authors' previous work (Mittra et al., 2015b).

claim: FISH analysis using multiple different pairs of human chromosome-specific FISH probes detected frequent co-localisation of red and green fluorescent signals.
source: We detected frequent co-localisation of red and green fluorescent signals suggesting that unrelated chromosomal fragments containing disparate DNA sequences had randomly amalgamated with each other to form highly complex concatemers (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Unrelated chromosomal fragments containing disparate DNA sequences had randomly amalgamated with each other to form highly complex concatemers.
source: We detected frequent co-localisation of red and green fluorescent signals suggesting that unrelated chromosomal fragments containing disparate DNA sequences had randomly amalgamated with each other to form highly complex concatemers (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of FISH signals shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some of the concatemers appeared strikingly prominent, suggesting that the components of the concatemer had been markedly amplified.
source: Some of the concatemers appeared strikingly prominent, which is particularly evident from images presented in Figure 3a. This suggested that the components of the concatemer had been markedly amplified.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the visual appearance of concatemers in Figure 3a.

claim: The analytical resolution of a FISH signal under a fluorescent microscope is in the range of 100–200 Kb.
source: As the analytical resolution of a FISH signal under a fluorescent microscope is in the range of 100–200 Kb (Cui et al., 2016), even the small concatemers can be assumed to be at least of a similar size range.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Cui et al., 2016).

claim: Even the small concatemers can be assumed to be at least 100–200 Kb in size.
source: As the analytical resolution of a FISH signal under a fluorescent microscope is in the range of 100–200 Kb (Cui et al., 2016), even the small concatemers can be assumed to be at least of a similar size range.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known resolution of FISH signals.

claim: Fluorescence signals of chromosome 4 co-localised with those of centromeres.
source: Surprisingly, we detected the fluorescence signals of chromosome 4 to co-localise with those of centromeres and of chromosome 22 to co-localise with those of telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a, panel 4.

claim: Fluorescence signals of chromosome 22 co-localised with those of telomeres.
source: Surprisingly, we detected the fluorescence signals of chromosome 4 to co-localise with those of centromeres and of chromosome 22 to co-localise with those of telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a, panel 5.

claim: Co-localising signals of telomeres and centromeres were detected.
source: Perhaps the ultimate evidence of the chaotic composition of the concatemers comes from our detection of co-localising signals of telomeres and centromeres (Figure 3a, panel 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a, panel 6.

claim: The centromeric signal seen in Figure 3a, panel 4 is strikingly prominent, suggesting that the concatemers had incorporated centromeric DNA sequences (171 bp in size) within their folds and that they had undergone large-scale amplification.
source: The centromeric signal seen in Figure 3a, panel 4 is strikingly prominent, suggesting that the concatemers had not only incorporated centromeric DNA sequences (171 bp in size) within their folds but that they had undergone large-scale amplification.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the visual appearance of the centromeric signal in Figure 3a, panel 4.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent signals generated upon treatment with FISH probes specific to different chromosome pairs ranged between 32.4% and 39.8%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent signals generated upon treatment with FISH probes specific to different chromosome pairs are given in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The extent of co-localisation ranged between 32.4% and 39.8%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Concatemerisation could also be detected in metaphase spreads prepared from serially passaged cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells.
source: Concatemerisation could also be detected in metaphase spreads prepared from serially passaged cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with human-specific FISH probes against chromosome 4 and chromosome 16.
source: Negative control experiments performed on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with human-specific FISH probes against chromosome 4 and chromosome 16 which were tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis using an antibody against histone H4 and a human whole genomic FISH probe detected numerous dually labelled signals representing concatemers.
source: Immuno-FISH analysis using an antibody against histone H4 and a human whole genomic FISH probe on chromatin fibres prepared from cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells in continuous passage. We detected numerous dually labelled signals representing concatemers which exhibited extensive structural and size variability, as well as remarkably variable spatial relationships with mouse chromatin fibres (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Concatemers exhibited extensive structural and size variability.
source: We detected numerous dually labelled signals representing concatemers which exhibited extensive structural and size variability, as well as remarkably variable spatial relationships with mouse chromatin fibres (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Concatemers exhibited remarkably variable spatial relationships with mouse chromatin fibres.
source: We detected numerous dually labelled signals representing concatemers which exhibited extensive structural and size variability, as well as remarkably variable spatial relationships with mouse chromatin fibres (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Many concatemers were detected in the cytoplasm or to have aligned with long stretches of mouse DNA.
source: Many concatemers were detected in the cytoplasm or to have aligned with long stretches of mouse DNA, while others exhibited unusual conformations or were seen to be dangling from the mouse DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Some concatemers exhibited unusual conformations or were seen to be dangling from the mouse DNA.
source: Many concatemers were detected in the cytoplasm or to have aligned with long stretches of mouse DNA, while others exhibited unusual conformations or were seen to be dangling from the mouse DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A similar peculiar conformation was found in clone D5 which had been developed several years earlier by treatment of NIH3T3 cells with cfChPs isolated from sera of cancer patients and which had undergone numerous passages and multiple freeze–thaw cycles.
source: A similar peculiar conformation was found in clone D5 which had been developed several years earlier by treatment of NIH3T3 cells with cfChPs isolated from sera of cancer patients and which had undergone numerous passages and multiple freeze–thaw cycles (Mittra et al., 2015b; Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and a citation to previous work (Mittra et al., 2015b).

claim: Concatemers persist across cell generations, showing remarkable stability.
source: This finding suggested that concatemers persist across cell generations, showing remarkable stability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of concatemers in clone D5 after numerous passages and freeze-thaw cycles.

claim: The fluorescent signals of the concatemers were strikingly prominent, suggesting that they greatly exceeded the threshold of detection of FISH signals (100–200 kb).
source: The fluorescent signals of the concatemers were also strikingly prominent, suggesting that they greatly exceeded the threshold of detection of FISH signals (100–200 kb; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the visual appearance of fluorescent signals and knowledge of FISH signal detection thresholds (Cui et al., 2016).

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localisation of the fluorescent signals of BrdU and DNA, indicating that the concatemers were actively synthesising DNA.
source: Cells in continuous passage were pulse-labelled with BrdU followed by immuno-FISH analysis using an antibody against BrdU and a human genomic DNA probe. The analysis revealed co-localisation of the fluorescent signals of BrdU and DNA, indicating that the concatemers were actively synthesising DNA (Figure 5a, upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a, upper panel.

claim: Immuno-FISH experiments revealed that the concatemers expressed human DNA polymerase γ.
source: Immuno-FISH experiments further revealed that the concatemers expressed human DNA polymerase γ (Figure 5a, middle panel)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a, middle panel.

claim: Dual immunofluorescence staining using antibodies against BrdU and human-specific DNA polymerase γ revealed co-localised signals, indicating that the concatemers had the potential to autonomously replicate themselves.
source: while dual immunofluorescence staining using antibodies against BrdU and human-specific DNA polymerase γ revealed co-localised signals, indicating that the concatemers had the potential to autonomously replicate themselves (Figure 5a, lower panel).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of BrdU and DNA polymerase γ signals shown in Figure 5a, lower panel.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and BrdU; human DNA and human DNA polymerase γ; and BrdU and human DNA polymerase γ ranged between 82.0% and 88.8%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and BrdU; human DNA and human DNA polymerase γ; and BrdU and human DNA polymerase γ are given in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The extent of co-localisation ranged between 82.0% and 88.8%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multiple co-localising signals of human DNA and BrdU, human DNA and human DNA polymerase γ, and BrdU and human DNA polymerase γ were detected in the extrachromosomal spaces on metaphase preparations from serially passaged cfChP-treated NIH3T3 cells.
source: These findings were confirmed on metaphase preparations from serially passaged cfChP-treated NIH3T3 cells, wherein we detected multiple co-localising signals of human DNA and BrdU, human DNA and human DNA polymerase γ, and BrdU and human DNA polymerase γ in the extrachromosomal spaces (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with either the human genomic DNA probe or the antibody against human DNA polymerase γ.
source: Negative control experiments performed on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with either to the human genomic DNA probe or the antibody against human DNA polymerase γ (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number of human FISH signals per chromosome at passage 198 was 4.07 times higher than those in passage 2.
source: The result showed that human FISH signals on mouse chromosomes increased progressively such that the number of signals at passage 198 was 4.07 times higher than those in passage 2 (Figure 6a).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The increase in mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) per chromosome between passage 2 and 198 was 237.2-fold.
source: We found that the increase in MFI between passage 2 and 198 was 237.2-fold (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The concatemers increased their copy number and extensively amplified themselves with time in culture.
source: Taken together, these results indicated that the concatemers increased their copy number and extensively amplified themselves with time in culture.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing increased FISH signals and MFI over passages.

claim: The vast majority of the concatemers either reacted exclusively with antibodies against H3K4me3 (open chromatin) or were hybrids of H3K4me3 and H3K9me3.
source: We found that the vast majority of the concatemers either reacted exclusively with antibodies against H3K4me3 (open chromatin) or were hybrids of H3K4me3 and H3K9me3, with only a small fraction of reacting exclusively with H3K9me3 (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Only a small fraction of concatemers reacted exclusively with H3K9me3.
source: We found that the vast majority of the concatemers either reacted exclusively with antibodies against H3K4me3 (open chromatin) or were hybrids of H3K4me3 and H3K9me3, with only a small fraction of reacting exclusively with H3K9me3 (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The concatemers contained open chromatin irrespective of whether the regions of the host mouse DNA reacted with antibodies against H3K4me3 or H3K9me3.
source: The figure also shows that the concatemers contained open chromatin irrespective of whether the regions of the host mouse DNA reacted with antibodies against H3K4me3 or H3K9me3.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Concatemers primarily contained nucleosome-depleted regions.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that concatemers primarily contained nucleosome-depleted regions and could bind to protein factors that facilitate gene transcription (Thomas et al., 2011) and DNA replication (MacAlpine et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the epigenetic analysis data and supported by citations (Thomas et al., 2011; MacAlpine et al., 2010).

claim: Concatemers could bind to protein factors that facilitate gene transcription.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that concatemers primarily contained nucleosome-depleted regions and could bind to protein factors that facilitate gene transcription (Thomas et al., 2011) and DNA replication (MacAlpine et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the epigenetic analysis data and supported by a citation (Thomas et al., 2011).

claim: Concatemers could bind to protein factors that facilitate DNA replication.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that concatemers primarily contained nucleosome-depleted regions and could bind to protein factors that facilitate gene transcription (Thomas et al., 2011) and DNA replication (MacAlpine et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the epigenetic analysis data and supported by a citation (MacAlpine et al., 2010).

claim: Abundant RNA was detected in the cytoplasm of cfChP-treated passaged cells, which was absent in the control NIH3T3 cells.
source: Using an assay kit which detects global RNA transcription, we detected abundant RNA in the cytoplasm of cfChP-treated passaged cells, which was absent in the control NIH3T3 cells (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The detection of RNA in the cytoplasm indicated that DNA contained within the concatemers was undergoing active transcription.
source: As RNA synthesis is normally restricted to the nucleus, the detection of RNA in the cytoplasm indicated that DNA contained within the concatemers was undergoing active transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of cytoplasmic RNA and knowledge that RNA synthesis is normally nuclear.

claim: Treatment of the cfChPs-treated passaged cells with actinomycin D abolished RNA synthesis.
source: Treatment of the cfChPs-treated passaged cells with actinomycin D or maintaining the cells at low temperature (31 °C) abolished RNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Maintaining the cfChPs-treated passaged cells at low temperature (31 °C) abolished RNA synthesis.
source: Treatment of the cfChPs-treated passaged cells with actinomycin D or maintaining the cells at low temperature (31 °C) abolished RNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: RNA synthesis by concatemers is dependent on active cellular metabolism.
source: These data indicated that the concatemers were actively involved in RNA synthesis, which is dependent on active cellular metabolism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the abolishment of RNA synthesis by actinomycin D and low temperature.

claim: Dual-FISH analysis revealed strictly co-localised signals of human genomic DNA and human ribosomal RNA, indicating that the concatemers were synthesising ribosomal RNA.
source: Dual FISH analysis on chromatin fibres prepared from serially passaged cfChP-treated cells revealed strictly co-localised signals, indicating that the concatemers were synthesising ribosomal RNA (Figure 9a, upper panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9a, upper panel.

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localised fluorescent signals generated by a human-specific genomic DNA probe and antibodies against RNA polymerase III.
source: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localised fluorescent signals generated by a human-specific genomic DNA probe and antibodies against RNA polymerase III and ribosomal protein (Figure 9a, middle and lower panels, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9a, middle panel.

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localised fluorescent signals generated by a human-specific genomic DNA probe and antibodies against ribosomal protein.
source: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localised fluorescent signals generated by a human-specific genomic DNA probe and antibodies against RNA polymerase III and ribosomal protein (Figure 9a, middle and lower panels, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9a, lower panel.

claim: Concatemers could autonomously synthesise critical components of the protein synthetic machinery.
source: These findings indicated that concatemers could autonomously synthesise critical components of the protein synthetic machinery.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of human DNA with ribosomal RNA, RNA polymerase III, and ribosomal protein.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and human ribosomal RNA; human DNA and RNA polymerase III; and human DNA and ribosomal protein ranged between 77.2% and 81.4%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and human ribosomal RNA; human DNA and RNA polymerase III; and human DNA and ribosomal protein are given in Figure 9—figure supplement 2. The extent of co-localisation ranged between 77.2% and 81.4%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Co-localisation of human DNA with ribosomal RNA, RNA polymerase III, and ribosomal protein was confirmed in metaphase preparations from serially passaged cells.
source: We confirmed these findings in metaphase preparations from serially passaged cells for all three components of the protein synthetic machinery mentioned above (Figure 9b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with the human-specific probes against DNA, ribosomal RNA, and the human-specific antibodies against RNA polymerase III and ribosomal protein.
source: Negative control experiments performed on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not react with the human-specific probes against DNA, ribosomal RNA, and the human-specific antibodies against RNA polymerase III and ribosomal protein (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claim: The fluorescent signals of various proteins frequently co-localised with those of human DNA, suggesting that the concatemers were capable of synthesising proteins.
source: We found that the fluorescent signals of the various proteins frequently co-localised with those of human DNA, suggesting that the concatemers were capable of synthesising proteins (Figure 10a).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of protein and DNA signals shown in Figure 10a.

claim: The newly synthesised proteins consistently remained associated with the concatemers of their origin.
source: Significantly, the newly synthesised proteins consistently remained associated with the concatemers of their origin (identified by fluorescent human DNA signals).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of protein and DNA signals.

claim: The concatemers apparently lacked the machinery required for protein sorting.
source: This finding suggested that, although the concatemers contained the critical components of a protein synthetic machinery, they apparently lacked the machinery required for protein sorting.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that proteins remained associated with concatemers.

claim: All the proteins detected seemed to be over-expressed, confirming that the gene segments corresponding to the proteins within the concatemers were amplified.
source: It should be noted that all the proteins that we detected seemed to be over-expressed, confirming that the gene segments corresponding to the proteins within the concatemers were amplified.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed over-expression of proteins.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and of various human proteins varied between 70.0% and 72.6%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent signals of human DNA and of various human proteins are given in Figure 10—figure supplement 1. The extent of co-localisation varied between 70.0% and 72.6%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-localisation of human DNA and various human proteins was confirmed in metaphase preparations from serially passaged cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells.
source: We further confirmed these findings in metaphase preparations from serially passaged cfChPs-treated NIH3T3 cells (Figure 10b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10b.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment did not show any positive fluorescent signals when treated with a variety of human-specific antibodies.
source: We also conducted extensive control experiments on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment using a variety of human-specific antibodies and found that none of them showed any positive fluorescent signals (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: The disparate DNA sequences that comprise the concatemers are transcribed and translated to generate proteins corresponding to the diverse DNA sequences that they contain apparently using their own protein synthetic machinery.
source: The above results indicated that the disparate DNA sequences that comprise the concatemers are transcribed and translated to generate proteins corresponding to the diverse DNA sequences that they contain apparently using their own protein synthetic machinery.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of various proteins co-localised with human DNA and the presence of protein synthetic machinery components.

claim: Dual-immunofluorescence experiments using pairs of antibodies against proteins, the corresponding genes of which were located on different chromosomes, revealed that the fluorescent signals frequently co-localised.
source: Dual-immunofluorescence experiments using pairs of antibodies against proteins, the corresponding genes of which were located on different chromosomes, revealed that the fluorescent signals frequently co-localised.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The proteins synthesised by the concatemers were fusion proteins with potentially novel functions.
source: This finding indicated that the proteins synthesised by the concatemers were fusion proteins with potentially novel functions (Figure 11).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of signals from antibodies against proteins encoded by genes on different chromosomes.

claim: Fusion proteins were detected both on chromatin fibres and metaphase preparations.
source: Fusion proteins were detected both on chromatin fibres and metaphase preparations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11a and 11b.

claim: The extent of co-localising signals indicative of fusion proteins ranged between 33.0% and 36.3%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent signals indicative of fusion proteins are shown in Figure 11a. The extent of co-localising signals ranged between 33.0% and 36.3% (Figure 11—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 11—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reverse transcriptase and transposase were found to co-localise with Bcl2 and cMyc, respectively.
source: Among the fusion proteins shown in Figure 11 we accidentally found reverse transcriptase and transposase to co-localise with Bcl2 and cMyc, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The concatemers might harbour gene components related to transposable elements.
source: This finding raised the possibility that the concatemers might harbour gene components related to transposable elements.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of reverse transcriptase and transposase.

claim: Dual-FISH experiments using a human genomic DNA probe and those targeting human LINE-1 and Alu showed that many of the fluorescent signals had co-localised indicating that the concatemers harboured DNA sequences of retro-transposable elements.
source: Dual-FISH experiments using a human genomic DNA probe and those targeting human LINE-1 and Alu showed that many of the fluorescent signals had co-localised indicating that the concatemers harboured DNA sequences of retro-transposable elements (Figure 12a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12a.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human DNA and human LINE-1 on chromatin fibres was 70.4%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human DNA and human LINE-1 and Alu on chromatin fibres are given in Figure 12—figure supplement 2. The extent of co-localisation was 70.4% and 72.8% for LINE-1 and Alu, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human DNA and human Alu on chromatin fibres was 72.8%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human DNA and human LINE-1 and Alu on chromatin fibres are given in Figure 12—figure supplement 2. The extent of co-localisation was 70.4% and 72.8% for LINE-1 and Alu, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar co-localising signals of human DNA and LINE-1/Alu were also seen on metaphase preparations.
source: Similar co-localising signals were also seen on metaphase preparations (Figure 12b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 12b.

claim: Both LINE-1 and Alu signals were extensively amplified.
source: The fact that both LINE-1 and Alu signals could be clearly detected by FISH analysis indicated that they were extensively amplified, given that LINE-1 and Alu are approximately 6000 bp and 300 bp in size, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detectability of FISH signals and knowledge of the sizes of LINE-1 and Alu elements.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment using human LINE-1 and Alu probes did not reveal any positive signals.
source: Control experiments performed on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment using human LINE-1 and Alu probes did not reveal any positive signals (Figure 12—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 12—figure supplement 3.

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis revealed co-localised signals of LINE-1 and Alu with human reverse transcriptase and transposase, indicating that the enzymes reverse transcriptase and transposase were frequently associated with DNA sequences corresponding to LINE-1 and Alu.
source: Immuno-FISH analysis using antibodies against human reverse transcriptase and transposase and FISH probes against LINE-1 and Alu revealed co-localised signals, indicating that the enzymes reverse transcriptase and transposase were frequently associated with DNA sequences corresponding to LINE-1 and Alu (Figure 13a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 13a and b.

claim: The association of LINE-1 and Alu with reverse transcriptase and transposase could potentially allow the transposable elements to re-arrange themselves on the mouse cell genome by translocating themselves from one location to another.
source: Such an association could potentially allow the transposable elements to re-arrange themselves on the mouse cell genome by translocating themselves from one location to another.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the association of transposable elements with enzymes involved in transposition.

claim: The extent of co-localisation on chromatin fibres of fluorescent FISH signals of human LINE-1 and human reverse transcriptase and transposase; and Alu and human reverse transcriptase and transposase ranged between 34.4% and 36.1%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation on chromatin fibres of fluorescent FISH signals of human LINE-1 and human reverse transcriptase and transposase; and Alu and human reverse transcriptase and transposase are given in Figure 13—figure supplement 1. The extent of co-localisation ranged between 34.4% and 36.1%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 1.

claim: Native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment using human-specific antibodies against reverse transcriptase and transposase and FISH probes against h-LINE-1 and h-ALU did not reveal any positive signals.
source: Control experiments performed on native NIH3T3 cells that had not been exposed to cfChPs treatment using human-specific antibodies against reverse transcriptase and transposase and FISH probes against h-LINE-1 and h-ALU did not reveal any positive signals (Figure 13—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 13—figure supplement 2.

claim: Transposable elements are known to increase their copy number with time.
source: As transposable elements are known to increase their copy number with time (Li et al., 2013), we were curious to find out whether the LINE-1 and Alu elements would proliferate and increase their copy number with progressively increasing passages.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Li et al., 2013).

claim: Immuno-FISH experiments detected co-localised signals of LINE-1 and Alu with human DNA polymerase γ, indicating that LINE-1 and Alu elements were associated with DNA polymerase.
source: Immuno-FISH experiments using antibodies against human DNA polymerase γ and FISH probes against LINE-1 and Alu detected co-localised signals, indicating that LINE-1 and Alu elements were associated with DNA polymerase, raising the possibility that they may have the potential to proliferate (Figure 14a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 14a and b.

claim: LINE-1 and Alu elements may have the potential to proliferate.
source: Immuno-FISH experiments using antibodies against human DNA polymerase γ and FISH probes against LINE-1 and Alu detected co-localised signals, indicating that LINE-1 and Alu elements were associated with DNA polymerase, raising the possibility that they may have the potential to proliferate (Figure 14a and b).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the association of LINE-1 and Alu with DNA polymerase.

claim: Immuno-FISH analysis of cells in continuous passage that had been pulse-labelled with BrdU showed co-localised signals generated by antibodies against BrdU and FISH probes against LINE-1 and Alu.
source: Immuno-FISH analysis of cells in continuous passage that had been pulse-labelled with BrdU showed co-localised signals generated by antibodies against BrdU and FISH probes against LINE-1 and Alu.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 14.

claim: The DNA of both LINE-1 and Alu transposable elements had the potential to replicate.
source: Taken together, these findings supported the idea that the DNA of both the transposable elements had the potential to replicate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of LINE-1 and Alu with BrdU and DNA polymerase.

claim: The extent of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human LINE-1 and human DNA polymerase and BrdU; and Alu and human DNA polymerase and BrdU varied between 35.8% and 36.9%.
source: Results of quantitative analysis of the degree of co-localisation of fluorescent FISH signals of human LINE-1 and human DNA polymerase and BrdU; and Alu and human DNA polymerase and BrdU are given in Figure 14—figure supplement 1. The extent of co-localisation varied between 35.8% and 36.9%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 14—figure supplement 1.

claim: The numbers of human LINE-1 signals per chromosome increased steadily between passage 2 and 198, resulting in a 7.6-fold increase in copy number.
source: Our results showed that the numbers of human LINE-1 and Alu signals per chromosome increased steadily between passage 2 and 198, resulting in a 7.6-fold increase in copy number in the case of LINE-1 and a 6.7-fold increase in the case of Alu (Figure 15a).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 15a.

claim: The numbers of human Alu signals per chromosome increased steadily between passage 2 and 198, resulting in a 6.7-fold increase in copy number.
source: Our results showed that the numbers of human LINE-1 and Alu signals per chromosome increased steadily between passage 2 and 198, resulting in a 7.6-fold increase in copy number in the case of LINE-1 and a 6.7-fold increase in the case of Alu (Figure 15a).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 15a.

claim: LINE-1 and Alu elements progressively increased their copy numbers by retrotransposition over time in the mouse genome.
source: These data indicated that LINE-1 and Alu elements progressively increased their copy numbers by retrotransposition over time in the mouse genome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing increased copy numbers of LINE-1 and Alu over passages.

claim: The increase in mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of LINE-1 signals per chromosome between passage 2 and 198 was 151.3-fold.
source: We found that the increase in MFI between passage 2 and 198 was 151.3-fold in the case of LINE-1 and 83.4-fold in the case of Alu (Figure 15b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 15b.

claim: The increase in mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of Alu signals per chromosome between passage 2 and 198 was 83.4-fold.
source: We found that the increase in MFI between passage 2 and 198 was 151.3-fold in the case of LINE-1 and 83.4-fold in the case of Alu (Figure 15b).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 15b.

claim: The transposable elements could not only proliferate but also extensively amplify themselves, thereby becoming increasingly effective in modifying the host genome.
source: Taken together, these data indicated that the transposable elements could not only proliferate but also extensively amplify themselves, thereby becoming increasingly effective in modifying the host genome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing increased copy numbers and MFI of LINE-1 and Alu over passages.

claim: Four different cell lines (Vero, Dolly, B/CMBA.OV, and HEK293) had the ability to internalise cfChPs.
source: We detected the presence of human DNA and human LINE-1 signals in all the above cell lines indicating that all of them had the ability to internalise cfChPs (Figure 16).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 16.

claim: Horizontal transfer of cfChPs is likely to be a universal phenomenon.
source: This finding led us to the conclusion that horizontal transfer of cfChPs is likely to be a universal phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of cfChPs internalization in multiple cell lines from different species.

claim: The human long non-coding RNA probe aligned with the entire length of the human DNA with almost 100% coverage in HEK293 and MRC5 cells.
source: When we applied this RNA probe to chromatin fibres prepared from two human cell lines (HEK293 and MRC5), we found that the RNA probe aligned with the entire length of the human DNA with almost 100% coverage (Figure 17a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 17a.

claim: The human long non-coding RNA probe did not bind to NIH3T3 mouse DNA.
source: The human specificity of the RNA probe was confirmed by the demonstration that it did not bind to NIH3T3 mouse DNA (Figure 17a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 17a.

claim: The long non-coding RNA probe could be used as a substitute to detect human non-coding DNA.
source: This finding suggested that the long non-coding RNA probe could be used as a substitute to detect human non-coding DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that the RNA probe aligned with human DNA with almost 100% coverage.

claim: The internalised cfChPs concatemers reacted with probes against both human whole genomic DNA and human non-coding DNA, and their fluorescent signals co-localised to the extent of 98.2%.
source: We discovered that the internalised cfChPs concatemers reacted with probes against both human whole genomic DNA and human non-coding DNA, and their fluorescent signals co-localised to the extent of 98.2% (Figure 17b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 17b.

claim: Virtually all the cfChPs concatemers were composed of non-coding DNA.
source: This led us to the conclusion that virtually all the cfChPs concatemers were composed of non-coding DNA.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the 98.2% co-localisation of human DNA and non-coding DNA signals.

claim: The fluorescent signals of DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, and reverse transcriptase co-localised with those of non-coding DNA.
source: We found that the fluorescent signals of a selected set of target enzymes, viz. DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, and reverse transcriptase co-localised with those of non-coding DNA, as did BrdU signals representing DNA synthesis (Figure 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 18.

claim: BrdU signals representing DNA synthesis co-localised with those of non-coding DNA.
source: We found that the fluorescent signals of a selected set of target enzymes, viz. DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase, and reverse transcriptase co-localised with those of non-coding DNA, as did BrdU signals representing DNA synthesis (Figure 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 18.

claim: The fluorescence signals of LINE-1 and Alu co-localised with those of non-coding DNA.
source: As anticipated, the fluorescence signals of LINE-1 and Alu also co-localised with those of non-coding DNA (Figure 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 18.

claim: The degree of co-localisation with the biomarkers was similar irrespective of whether a whole human genomic probe or one against non-coding DNA was used.
source: The latter also shows that the degree of co-localisation with the biomarkers was similar irrespective of whether we used a whole human genomic probe (results of which are shown earlier) or the one against non-coding DNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 18—figure supplement 1.

claim: The biological activities of the concatemers are attributable to non-coding DNA.
source: Collectively, these findings provided confirmation that the biological activities of the concatemers are attributable to non-coding DNA and suggested that non-coding DNA has many unique biological functions which remain dormant but are activated following cellular apoptosis to become detectable in association with the cfChP concatemers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-localisation of biomarkers with non-coding DNA.

claim: Non-coding DNA has many unique biological functions which remain dormant but are activated following cellular apoptosis to become detectable in association with the cfChP concatemers.
source: Collectively, these findings provided confirmation that the biological activities of the concatemers are attributable to non-coding DNA and suggested that non-coding DNA has many unique biological functions which remain dormant but are activated following cellular apoptosis to become detectable in association with the cfChP concatemers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from the observed biological activities of concatemers composed of non-coding DNA.

claim: cfChPs from healthy individuals were readily internalised by NIH3T3 cells.
source: We found that cfChPs from healthy individuals were also readily internalised by NIH3T3 cells, wherein they behaved in a manner similar to that of cfChPs derived from the cancer patients (Figure 19).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 19.

claim: cfChPs from healthy individuals behaved in a manner similar to that of cfChPs derived from cancer patients.
source: We found that cfChPs from healthy individuals were also readily internalised by NIH3T3 cells, wherein they behaved in a manner similar to that of cfChPs derived from the cancer patients (Figure 19).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 19.

claim: cfChPs released from hypoxia-induced dying MDA-MB-231 cells could reciprocate all the intracellular activities and functions that were observed using cfChPs isolated from serum of both cancer patients and healthy individuals.
source: We observed that cfChPs that were released from hypoxia-induced dying MDA-MB-231 cells could reciprocate all the intracellular activities and functions that were observed using cfChPs isolated from serum of both cancer patients and healthy individuals (Figure 20).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 20.

claim: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) plays an important role in the adaptation of microorganisms to changing environments and in evolutionary processes.
source: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) plays an important role in the adaptation of microorganisms to changing environments and in evolutionary processes (Bushman, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bushman, 2002).

claim: Gene therapy is founded on the principle of HGT.
source: Indeed, gene therapy is founded on the principle of HGT, and several studies have indicated that oncogenes can be horizontally transferred across mammalian cells (Anker et al., 1994; Bergsmedh et al., 2001; Dvořáková et al., 2013; García-Olmo et al., 2010; Trejo-Becerril et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Several studies have indicated that oncogenes can be horizontally transferred across mammalian cells.
source: Indeed, gene therapy is founded on the principle of HGT, and several studies have indicated that oncogenes can be horizontally transferred across mammalian cells (Anker et al., 1994; Bergsmedh et al., 2001; Dvořáková et al., 2013; García-Olmo et al., 2010; Trejo-Becerril et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: HGT may occur naturally in mammalian cells and contributes to evolutionary, and potentially oncogenic, processes.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that HGT may occur naturally in mammalian cells and contributes to evolutionary, and potentially oncogenic, processes.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Approximately 40% of the human genome is composed of retro-transposable elements.
source: The sequencing of the human genome has revealed that approximately 40% of the genome is composed of retro-transposable elements (Lander et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Lander et al., 2001).

claim: Retro-transposable elements have been shown to numerically increase with age.
source: and the latter has been shown to numerically increase with age (De Cecco et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (De Cecco et al., 2013).

claim: Retro-transposable elements are implicated in cancer due to their ability to create genomic structural variation, alterations, and instability.
source: It should be mentioned in this context that retro-transposable elements are implicated in cancer due to their ability to create genomic structural variation, alterations, and instability (Burns, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Burns, 2017).

claim: Illegitimate and repeated genomic integration of cfChPs may be the underlying aetiological factor for cancer as well as ageing and age-related chronic diseases.
source: We have earlier hypothesised that illegitimate and repeated genomic integration of cfChPs may be the underlying aetiological factor for cancer as well as ageing and age-related chronic diseases (Raghuram et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from the authors' previous work (Raghuram et al., 2019).

claim: Transposable elements carried by the concatemers may play a significant role in mammalian evolution by inserting themselves into unpredictable locations, disrupting or restoring gene function, generating new regulatory elements, and potentially inducing genomic rearrangements and instability.
source: Transposable elements carried by the concatemers may also play a significant role in mammalian evolution by inserting themselves into unpredictable locations, disrupting or restoring gene function, generating new regulatory elements, and potentially inducing genomic rearrangements and instability (Senft and Macfarlan, 2021; Pourrajab and Hekmatimoghaddam, 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to published research (Senft and Macfarlan, 2021; Pourrajab and Hekmatimoghaddam, 2021).

claim: Many transposable elements are thought to represent remnants of ancient viruses that had become integrated into host genomes millions of years earlier.
source: Many transposable elements are thought to represent remnants of ancient viruses that had become integrated into host genomes millions of years earlier (Gilbert and Feschotte, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gilbert and Feschotte, 2018).

claim: The concatemers carry LINE-1 and Alu elements, suggesting transposable elements are 'foreign' genetic elements that are acquired from dying cells via HGT.
source: Our demonstration that the concatemers carry LINE-1 and Alu elements suggests transposable elements are 'foreign' genetic elements that are acquired from dying cells via HGT.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the detection of LINE-1 and Alu in concatemers.

claim: Generation of novel proteins resulting from gene duplication, sequence divergence, and gene combination may have evolutionary functions.
source: It has been proposed that generation of novel proteins resulting from gene duplication, sequence divergence, and gene combination may also have evolutionary functions (Bashton and Chothia, 2007; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bashton and Chothia, 2007; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: The plethora of novel fusion proteins discovered may play a role in the evolutionary process.
source: We speculate that the plethora of novel fusion proteins that we discovered may likewise play a role in the evolutionary process.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on inference from the detection of fusion proteins.

claim: HGT occurs in mammalian cells via cfChPs released from the billions of host cells that die on a daily basis.
source: Our results suggest that HGT occurs in mammalian cells via cfChPs released from the billions of host cells that die on a daily basis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: Circulating cfChPs released from dying cells function as a new class of mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that act intra-corporeally and transfer themselves horizontally to the organism's own cells.
source: We previously proposed that circulating cfChPs released from dying cells function as a new class of mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that act intra-corporeally and transfer themselves horizontally to the organism's own cells (Mittra, 2015a).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis from the authors' previous work (Mittra, 2015a).

claim: 'Within-self' HGT may occur in mammals on a massive scale via the medium of cfChP concatemers that have undergone extensive and complex modifications resulting in their behaviour as 'foreign' genetic elements.
source: Thus, 'within-self' HGT may occur in mammals on a massive scale via the medium of cfChP concatemers that have undergone extensive and complex modifications resulting in their behaviour as 'foreign' genetic elements.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from the study's findings.

claim: Whole genome sequencing on Illumina GA IIX platform and bioinformatics analysis of two single cell clones (D5 and B2) developed from the cfChPs treated cells detected 25,000–28,000 strictly human reads in the mouse cell genomes.
source: Whole genome sequencing on Illumina GA IIX platform and bioinformatics analysis of two single cell clones (D5 and B2) developed from the cfChPs treated cells detected 25,000–28,000 strictly human reads in the mouse cell genomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to whole genome sequencing data from the authors' previous work.

claim: Computational analysis of the two clones detected 35–47 unique human Alu repeat sequences in the recipient cells which were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing.
source: Computational analysis of the two clones also detected 35–47 unique human Alu repeat sequences in the recipient cells which were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to computational analysis and sequencing data from the authors' previous work.

claim: ecDNA can be a source of extreme gene amplification enabling a cell to harbour multiple copies of oncogenes.
source: In particular, it has been suggested that ecDNA can be a source of extreme gene amplification enabling a cell to harbour multiple copies of oncogenes and can potentially promote tumour heterogeneity and therapy resistance (Wu et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Wu et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2024).

claim: ecDNA can potentially promote tumour heterogeneity and therapy resistance.
source: In particular, it has been suggested that ecDNA can be a source of extreme gene amplification enabling a cell to harbour multiple copies of oncogenes and can potentially promote tumour heterogeneity and therapy resistance (Wu et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Wu et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2024).

claim: It is believed that ecDNAs are derived from the host cell's own genome resulting from chromothripsis, DNA damage, or genomic instability.
source: It is believed that ecDNAs are derived from the host cell's own genome resulting from chromothripsis, DNA damage, or genomic instability (Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Wu et al., 2022).

claim: ecDNAs that have been detected in human cancers may represent concatemers composed of cfChPs acquired from surrounding dying cancer cells via HGT.
source: Our study, which also detected multiple highly amplified oncogene products, often appearing as fusion proteins, raises the possibility that ecDNAs that have been detected in human cancers may represent concatemers composed of cfChPs acquired from surrounding dying cancer cells via HGT.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the study's findings.

claim: A cell simultaneously harbours two genome forms that function independently of each other: one that is inherited (hereditary genome) and numerous others that are acquired (satellite genomes).
source: In summary, the present findings lead to a novel hypothesis that a cell simultaneously harbours two genome forms that function independently of each other: one that is inherited (hereditary genome) and numerous others that are acquired (satellite genomes).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the study's findings.

claim: The satellite genomes may potentially perform evolutionary functions by acting as vehicles of transposable elements and generating a plethora of novel proteins.
source: The satellite genomes may potentially perform evolutionary functions by acting as vehicles of transposable elements and generating a plethora of novel proteins.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the study's findings.

claim: The biological life of the genome is not co-terminus with the death of a cell, but rather the genome is recycled in a fragmented and extensively modified incarnation to perform new functions in distant destinations acting as 'within-self' foreign genetic elements.
source: Our findings suggest that the biological life of the genome is not a co-terminus with the death of a cell, but rather that the genome is recycled in a fragmented and extensively modified incarnation to perform new functions in distant destinations acting as 'within-self' foreign genetic elements.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from the study's findings.

claim: A cell's propensity to internalise cfChPs represents a natural biological process designed to modify the hereditary genome, which in turn may promote evolutionary change.
source: This suggests that a cell's propensity to internalise cfChPs represents a natural biological process designed to modify the hereditary genome, which in turn may promote evolutionary change.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the study's findings.

claim: Mammalian evolution is driven by 'within-self' HGT of cfChP concatemers that have undergone such extensive and complex modifications that they behave as 'foreign' genetic elements.
source: We hypothesise that mammalian evolution is driven by 'within-self' HGT of cfChP concatemers that have undergone such extensive and complex modifications that they behave as 'foreign' genetic elements.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the study's findings.
